alice: Proposal: let's standardize a bench protocol for kernel selection + batching + KV-cache behavior. Short version: define traffic profiles, require explicit warmup/cache-fill, report TTFT and TPOT separately, and always run both synthetic and replay with the same seq-length distribution.

ben: +1. Can we be explicit about warmup? how long, and do we need separate cache-warm vs runtime-warm cycles?

alice: Good call. My suggestion: two-phase warmup: 1) cold-start compile/warm (30–60s with low qps to trigger jit/compilation), 2) cache-fill using representative request set until KV hit-rate stabilizes (monitor kv_hits/kv_lookups). Document the dataset used.

carmen: Also add a separate micro-benchmark for kernel selection determinism. Run each kernel candidate with identical inputs and record p50/p95/p99 for a few sequence lengths (32, 256, 1024). That lets us isolate kernel perf from batching heuristics.

dave: sharing a quick profiling snippet that caught a regression last week — note the spike in memcpy during batching path:

```
# perf top sample
Samples: 20K of event 'cycles'
  23.4%  runtime.so  [.] batching::dispatch
  12.1%  runtime.so  [.] kv_cache::read_batch
   9.8%  libc.so     [.] memcpy
   4.3%  cudnn.so    [.] conv_kernel
```
We should capture flamegraphs after each run (before/after batching change).

eva: On metrics: can we be stricter about TTFT vs TPOT? We keep mixing them. My proposal: TTFT = time from HTTP request accepted to first token byte out. TPOT = total useful tokens / end-to-end time (exclude leading prompt tokens if we pre-send them). Also report tokens/sec (goodput) and raw QPS.

ben: Agree. Add that we should report both median and tail latencies (p50,p95,p99) for TTFT and per-token latency where applicable. For goodput include breakdown: delivered tokens vs wasted tokens (retries, rerolls).

alice: For apples-to-apples between synthetic & replay: force the replay harness to sample inputs to match the synthetic seq-length histogram and prompt distribution. If we replay recorded traffic, capture original timestamps but allow compression factor for throughput scaling. Document compression.

carmen: One more: batching heuristics should have an "equal-work" baseline where we limit batch by token-length sum instead of by count. That often changes kernel selection behavior. Run both.

loadbot: loadtest-started: run_id=bench-2026-03-12-14-00 profile=short-mix workers=64 target_qps=2000

dave: After the run, extract these artifacts into the benchmark run directory: metrics.json, traces.pb, flamegraph.svg, kernel_decisions.csv, kv_stats.csv, and a short readme with the exact model binary + commit hash. If something is missing, the run is not comparable.

eva: Concern: synthetic traffic usually underestimates cold-cache penalties. Recommend we include a 'cold-run' mode where we restart the runtime between samples or flush KV cache explicitly. Compare cold vs warm numbers.

alice: Agreed. The protocol will require: cold_run (restart or flush), warm_run (cache-fill), and steady_run (sustained qps). Each run type must include raw traces.

ben: Regression detection: run a quick diff script to compare p95 TTFT and TPOT against baseline; alert if TTFT_p95 regresses >5% or TPOT drops >7% relative. Keep the thresholds configurable per model.

carmen: For fairness across hardware: normalize goodput by effective GPU memory bandwidth and flops where possible, and include kernel-level counters (sm_efficiency) to explain differences.

alice: I'll draft a one-pager with the exact commands, example config, and artifact list. Outline: traffic profiles, warmup rules, run types, measured metrics (TTFT/TPOT/p50/p95/p99/goodput/QPS), artifact collection, and regression thresholds. Any objections?

ben: none from me. please include sample CLI snippets for the replay harness.

alice: will do. Expect a PR by EOD. Thanks all :thumbsup:
